釘子提琴具有獨特而詭異的音色特徵。其音質介於弦樂器與打擊樂器之間，帶有刺耳而尖銳: The nail violin has a distinctive, eerie timbre. Its sound lies between string and percussion, with a harsh, sharp brightness shot through with a cold metallic quality. When the bow rubs the nails the result is grainy, like a violin but coarser and more textured. Its range is fairly limited, mostly in the upper middle register. Because the semicircular wooden soundboard resonates, the sound has a moderate ring and penetration. Against the warm elegance of the violin, the nail violin seems more primitive and wild; against the crispness of the xylophone it has the continuity and expression peculiar to strings. This rare and individual timbre makes it a natural choice for experimental music and contemporary works.

The early form was a semicircular wooden soundboard set with iron or brass nails, bowed to give a chromatic scale; an improved version, now in the Berlin Hochschule, has two crescent-shaped soundboxes, the upper row giving the diatonic scale and the lower the semitones. Around 1780 to 1790 the Bohemian musician Senal played it across Germany and added sympathetic strings, calling it the violino harmonico. Later came variants with glass or wooden rods, with a pedal keyboard, the Adiaphonon and the Stockspiel; today Michael Meadows has also made copies of the early design.

The nail violin is a friction idiophone invented in 1740 by the German violinist Johann Wilde, Hornbostel–Sachs 131.21. It is built as a semicircular wooden soundboard set with iron or brass nails of different lengths, which form a chromatic scale when bowed; the deeper a nail is driven in, the shorter the exposed part and the higher the pitch. The bow is strung with thick black horsehair and sounds by friction, and the nails or rods may also be struck. At the end of the eighteenth century the Bohemian player Senal travelled through Germany playing this instrument.
釘子提琴的琴身來源載明為半圓形木製音板，發聲體為長短不同的鐵釘或黃銅釘，以弓擦奏: The body of the nail violin is given in the sources as a semicircular wooden soundboard, and the sounding elements are iron or brass nails of different lengths, set sounding by the bow; the bow is strung with thick black horsehair. The improved type has two crescent-shaped soundboxes, with two rows of iron nails on the upper curved wall, giving the diatonic scale and the semitones respectively. There are also versions with glass or wooden rods in place of metal nails, and later designs bowed on steel bars or played with wooden rods and a rosin-coated glove. Apart from the wood, metal, glass and horsehair mentioned, the sources do not state the materials of the other parts.
